sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Mechanism**: In Hypermetropia, the **eyeball is too short** or the **cornea/lens curvature is too flat**, causing the focal point to shift behind the retina.
• **Correction**: A **Convex Lens** (converging lens) is placed in front of the eye to converge incoming light rays before they enter the eye, effectively shifting the focal point forward onto the retina.
• **Near Point**: The 'near point' of a hypermetropic eye is farther away than the normal 25 cm.
• **Key Metric**: The power of the corrective lens is always **positive (+)**, measured in Diopters (D).

items.definition: The ability of the eye to bend light; measured in Diopters. Hypermetropia requires additional positive power.
The light-sensitive inner lining of the eye where images must be focused for clear vision.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Corrective Eyewear**: Standard spectacles using convex lenses.
• **Public Health**: National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB) addresses refractive errors as a major cause of avoidable blindness.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Challenges**: Lack of screening in rural areas, high cost of specialized lenses.
• **Solutions**: Tele-ophthalmology, distribution of low-cost ready-to-wear spectacles.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'H-C-B' (Hypermetropia = Convex = Behind).
• **Decoded Meaning**: Hypermetropia is corrected by a Convex lens because the image forms Behind the retina.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often swaps 'Hypermetropia' with 'Myopia' in statements. Remember: Myopia = Concave (Near), Hypermetropia = Convex (Far).
Mains Value Addition: Mention 'Refractive Error' as a significant contributor to 'Avoidable Blindness' in India, linking it to SDG 3 (Good Health and Well-being).

keyTakeaways: Hypermetropia is caused by an eyeball that is too short or a lens that is too flat.
Convex lenses are used to converge light rays, moving the focal point onto the retina.
The corrective lens power for Hypermetropia is always positive.
